sentences.text: The generic name combines the Latin name for Dorset with the Greek word for Titan, while the specific name highlights a prominent deltopectoral crest on the humerus bone.
This long, sharply projecting crest sits on an entire humerus that is very strong, suggesting the front legs were longer than the hind legs.
The bone's unique construction led John Hulke to defend the hypothesis that sauropods lived on land rather than in the sea, as was commonly believed at the time.
The humerus measures 137 cm without the missing central piece, with an estimated total length of 160 cm, indicating a body length of about 18 meters and a weight of 12 tons.
The holotype fossil, a partial left upper arm bone, was discovered by R.I. Smith near Sandsfoot in Dorset, England.
The species was originally described in 1874 by John Hulke as a species of Cetiosaurus.
According to the describers, it is a member of the Titanosauriformes, a group that includes both Brachiosauridae and Titanosauria.

It lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 million years ago in the Kimmeridgian stage, in what is now Europe. The time range spans from the Kimmeridgian to the Berriasian, between 154.8 and 137.05 million years ago.
It is debated whether the animal belongs to the Brachiosauridae, as a 2007 hypothesis by Darren Naish and David Martill could not be supported by the describers with new features.
